claim: Dorado was aged in glass demijohns and part-filled barrels under a film of yeast, closer to a light Sherry than to any modern white.
because: The D.O. Rueda defines Rueda Dorado by crianza oxidativa (oxidative ageing), with at least the last two years before sale in oak barrel. Ageing under a film of yeast (crianza biologica) belongs to the other traditional style, Rueda Palido, which needs at least three years in oak. The explanation says Dorado aged under flor, which contradicts the keyed option itself ('an oxidatively aged white'), and a candidate would learn the two Rueda styles the wrong way round.
fix: Dorado was aged oxidatively, traditionally in glass demijohns left out in the sun and then in oak, with no film of yeast, so it was closer to an old Oloroso than to any modern white. Today's rule asks for at least two years in oak before sale; its biologically aged sibling, under flor, is Rueda Palido. A little of both is still made.
